info.bio:
Def Leppard es una banda británica originaria de Sheffield, Inglaterra, que comenzó a finales de los años 70, y que alcanzó su éxito en la década de los 80 acercando el heavy metal a las emisoras de radio y al gran público en general, gracias a la mezcla de rock melódico con un gran trabajo vocal.

El bajista Rick Savage, el guitarrista Pete Willis y el baterista Tony Kenning todos estudiantes de la escuela Tapton, en Sheffield, Reino Unido en el año 1977, se unen para formar la banda de rock “Atomic Mass”.

scenes.name: New Wave of British Heavy Metal
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Explosión de bandas nuevas en Gran Bretaña entre 1979 y 1981. No hay un estilo común: cada grupo es bastante único, pero todos comparten la sensibilidad heavy, la juventud y el énfasis en lo visual. Muchos siguen la tradición; otros se especializan en un rasgo del código. Iron Maiden y Def Leppard triunfan a lo grande, Venom persiste con un público reducido y la mayoría desaparece, aunque alguno, como Diamond Head (versionado por Metallica), deja huella. De sus innovaciones rítmicas sale directamente el thrash. Con ella llega el «renacimiento» del heavy de principios de los ochenta.

scenes.name: Lite metal: pop metal y glam
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El subgénero que, desde 1983-84, intensifica el polo melódico del heavy y lo mezcla con el hard rock, quitándole el grave grueso. Philip Bashe lo llamó «metal pop» y señaló a Def Leppard y Van Halen; otros ejemplos son Poison, Bon Jovi, Ratt y Cinderella. Sus detractores, el público tradicional y el del thrash, lo llaman «poseurs», «false metal», «nerf metal», «poodle bands» o «glam», motes que describen bien sus rasgos: falta de autenticidad, pelo cardado, ropa colorida en lugar del negro obrero. Voz dulce sin gruñidos, armonías al modo de Aerosmith y Kiss, letras de amor y lujuria con nombres de chica y, sobre todo, la power ballad, que entra en radios que excluían el heavy y gana público nuevo, como las versiones blancas de Pat Boone en los cincuenta. MTV impulsó mucho su desarrollo. Se queda con la herencia dionisíaca y elimina el caos: «lo realmente pesado se quita».

scenes.name: La edad de oro del heavy metal
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El heavy metal renace en los mismos años que la new wave, aprovechando los sellos independientes: Motörhead (puente entre metal, Stooges/MC5 y punk), Judas Priest, Iron Maiden, Diamond Head, Def Leppard y, en EE UU, Van Halen. Entre 1982 y 1985 el subgénero gótico se convierte en «black metal» (Venom, Mercyful Fate, Celtic Frost, Helloween, Bathory). El pop-metal y el shock-rock (Twisted Sister, Mötley Crüe, Joan Jett, Bon Jovi, Savatage); la pompa y el doom (Manowar, Voivod, Saint Vitus, Pentagram); el metal progresivo (Living Colour, Queensrÿche, King's X, Pantera, Joe Satriani) y el «street sound» de Los Ángeles (Guns N' Roses, Jane's Addiction, Faster Pussycat).

podcast.title: "Heavy Metal for People Who Think" Image
podcast.body: In the summer of 1983, a Grand Junction, Colorado, newspaper headline humorously dubbed Def Leppard "heavy metal for people who think," implying their sound was "safe, not scary like Black Sabbath." This image was reinforced by their "squeaky clean" appearance, featuring nicely tailored clothes and neatly styled 80s hair, which lead singer Joe Elliott attributed to their working-class upbringing and proud parents' emphasis on self-respect. "Deaf Leopard, heavy metal for people who think."

podcast.title: Drum Programming Challenges on "Pyromania"
podcast.body: For the album "Pyromania," producer Mutt Lange insisted on the latest technology for drums. Chris Berkett spent six weeks programming all the drums on a Fairlight CMI. This pre-MIDI process required converting the drummer's demo tapes into musical score and then typing every single event into the monophonic Fairlight using a mathematical music composition language. "And I had to write all that stuff out in score. Because it had to be converted to mathematical music language."

podcast.title: Inspired by Marc Bolan and T-Rex
podcast.body: Def Leppard was inspired by the character of Marc Bolan and the albums of T-Rex. Their music from the late 70s and 80s, both artistically and musically, is difficult to understand without the influence of Bolan and T-Rex. "para deflepar... es muy difícil entender el rock de final de los 70 y de los 80. Tanto a nivel artístico, como incluso a nivel musical, sin entender lo que fue el personaje de Marvolan y de lo que fueron estos iscos de T-Rex."

podcast.title: Joe Elliott on Band's Image
podcast.body: In a 1983 interview, lead singer Joe Elliott, with a charming northern English accent, stated, "that's just the way we are." He expressed that the band "never wanted to look like tramps," criticizing groups like Motorhead for appearing in "car mechanic overalls with unwashed hair," which he considered "abusing the audience." Elliott believed their "squeaky clean image" stemmed from their working-class roots and parents who instilled self-respect, ensuring they avoided looking disheveled. "He never wanted to look like tramps. Some of these bands like Motorhead just sort of turn up in their car mechanic overalls with unwashed hair. To me, that's really abusing the audience."

podcast.title: MTV Influence and Comparison
podcast.body: Joe Elliott later commented on MTV's influence on Def Leppard's career, suggesting that if MTV were credited for their success, the same could be said for artists like Michael Jackson or Peter Gabriel. He noted that Jackson and Gabriel, like Def Leppard, had established careers long before MTV's inception, implying MTV amplified existing talent rather than solely creating it. "Elliott responded years later that if you were going to credit MTV for Deaf Leopard's career, maybe you could say the same thing about Michael Jackson or Peter Gabriel."

podcast.title: Meticulous Drum Production on "Pyromania"
podcast.body: The drum programming for "Pyromania" was an incredibly meticulous process. Mutt Lange would spend half a day listening to a single hi-hat sound against a click track, checking if it was "a bit ahead, a bit behind," before approving it. "We would listen literally to a hi hat against the click for half a day."

podcast.title: Rejection of Heavy Metal Label
podcast.body: Def Leppard actively disliked being categorized as "heavy metal," fearing it would negatively impact their record sales. Joe Elliott specifically expressed displeasure at the music media lumping them in with bands like Motley Crue or Warrant, underscoring their desire to appeal to a broader audience beyond the traditional heavy metal fan base. "But in 1983 the band's image was such that they did not even want the heavy metal label for fear it would negatively affect record sales."

podcast.title: Repeated Drum Recording Due to Tape Wear on "Pyromania"
podcast.body: The drums for "Pyromania" had to be re-recorded three separate times from the original Fairlight floppy disks. This was because the analog 24-track master tapes, on which guitars and vocals were overdubbed, wore out through repeated transfers to new tapes, forcing the producer to request "first generation drums" again. "We've worn out three tapes doing all the guitars and the vocals. And they transferred... It wasn't digital in those days. It was analog. They transferred 24 track onto another new one because it was getting thin."

podcast.title: Steve Clark's Tragic Death
podcast.body: Steve Clark, one of Def Leppard's guitarists, tragically died in 1991 from a lethal combination of prescription drugs and alcohol. This event stands in stark contrast to Joe Elliott's earlier comments about the band's "squeaky clean image" and self-respect. "There is some sad irony in reading that now knowing that Steve Clark, one of Deaf Leopard's guitarists, died from a lethal combination of prescription drugs and alcohol in 1991."
